newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain - Sizeable new wheat crop seen.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain - Sizeable new wheat crop seen.

text.p: Official forecasts of Australia's 1997/98 wheat production appeared to under-estimate the likely crop, grains executives told Reuters on Friday.
The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) on Tuesday forecast Australia's new wheat crop at 17.82 million tonnes, up from an earlier forecast of 16.98 million tonnes.
Guy Allen, Grain Trading Manager of New South Wales (NSW) co-operative GrainCorp, said on Friday the new crop forecast appeared a little light, judging by feedback from growers.
"Most trade estimates tend to be up in the high 18 million tonnes, 19 million tonnes, that level," he said.

"We're getting good moisture profiles, particularly in central and northern NSW and Queensland. Victoria and southern NSW are a bit dry but that's not unusual for this time of year." Last year, projections of the 1996/97 Australian wheat crop by both the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) and ABARE initially considerably under-estimated production.
Early estimates put the 1996/97 wheat crop at 17.5 million tonnes. It turned out to be a record 23.5 million tonnes.

The focus shifted toward Australia's 1997/98 wheat crop prospects last week as shipments from the big current crop continued high, as domestic cash and futures wheat markets dried up for lack of supply and as pulses ran hot.

The AWB shipped 572,921 tonnes of wheat in the week to Friday, slightly ahead of the 515,626 million tonnes shipped in the previous week. This brought shipments for the October to September marketing year to 9.57 million tonnes, far ahead of the 6.43 million tonnes a year ago.
This took place against the background of a domestic cash and futures wheat markets which Graincorp's Allen described as "frustratingly quiet".
The smaller pulses markets, however, featured sales to India, where crop problems have sent prices rocketing, traders said.
One trader confirmed a sale of 30,000-40,000 tonnes of pulses in a deal worth about A$9 million. "Quite a lot of pulses for us," the trader, who asked not to be named, said.

An active but sensitive Indian chick pea market had jumped over the past eight weeks to peak at A$310 a tonne "track" (fob plus A$24 a tonne in delivery charges) from A$245, traders said. Prices edged back to about A$298 on Friday.
"There's been a very active trade in chick peas in the past two weeks," Peter Howard of New England Agricultural Traders, one of Australia's more active pulse sellers to India, said.

But cash wheat, in Allen's words, last week was "dead" after the AWB on Monday unexpectedly raised most wheat pool prices, with ASW up by A$2 to A$195 a tonne. Traders complained that AWB market dominance squeezed liquidity while the strong Australian
dollar kept markets defensive.

End users were not willing to pay and held comfortable supplies, while growers were expected to remain reluctant to sell until the new financial year began on July 1, Allen said. Despite the malaise, cash wheat prices remained firm with Australian Standard White (ASW) moving up to A$180 delivered Brisbane from A$175.
Milling wheats were a little firmer with Australian Hard bid at A$182 and Prime Hard at A$196 Newcastle.
Sorghum made the biggest gain of the week, rising by A$3-A$5 a tonne to A$165-A$166 Newcastle as demand spilled over the from the tight feed wheat market.
Feed barley was steady to slightly firmer. Now the cheapest feedgrain, barley sold at A$158-A$160 port equivalent.
Only three lots of Australian wheat futures sold last week in a string of tradeless days. Settlement prices stayed firm.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
